title: Reindeer
wiki_lead:
The reindeer or caribou (Rangifer tarandus) is a species of deer with circumpolar distribution, native to the Arctic, subarctic, tundra, boreal, and mountainous regions of Northern Europe, Siberia, and North America. It is the only representative of the genus Rangifer. More recent studies suggest the splitting of reindeer and caribou (North American terminology). "All caribou and reindeer throughout the world are considered to be the same species, but there are seven subspecies."
Reindeer occur in both migratory and sedentary populations, and their herd sizes vary greatly in different regions. The tundra subspecies are adapted for extreme cold, and some are adapted for long-distance migration.
Reindeer vary greatly in size and color from the smallest, the Svalbard reindeer (R. (t.) platyrhynchus), to the largest, Osborn's caribou (R. t. osborni). Although reindeer are quite numerous, some species and subspecies are in decline and considered vulnerable. They are unique among deer (Cervidae) in that females may have antlers, although the prevalence of antlered females varies by subspecies.
Reindeer are the only successfully semi-domesticated deer on a large scale in the world. Both wild and domestic reindeer (R. t. forma domesticus) have been an important source of food, clothing, and shelter for Arctic people from prehistoric times.  They are still herded and hunted today. In some traditional Christmas legends, Santa Claus's reindeer pull a sleigh through the night sky to help Santa Claus deliver gifts to good children on Christmas Eve.

Description
Names follow international convention before the recent revision (see Reindeer § Taxonomy below). Reindeer / caribou (Rangifer) vary in size from the smallest, the Svalbard reindeer (R. (t.) platyrhynchus), to the largest, Osborn's caribou (R. t. osborni). They also vary in coat color and antler architecture.
The North American range of caribou extends from Alaska through the Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut throughout the tundra, taiga (boreal forest) and south through the Canadian Rocky Mountains. Of the eight subspecies classified by Harding (2022) into the Arctic caribou (R. arcticus), the migratory mainland barren-ground caribou of Arctic Alaska and Northern Canada (R. t. arcticus), summer in tundra and winter in taiga, a transitional forest zone between boreal forest and tundra; the nomadic Peary caribou (R. t. pearyi) lives in the polar desert of the high Arctic Archipelago and Grant's caribou (R. t. granti also called the Porcupine caribou) lives in the western end of the Alaska Peninsula and the adjacent islands; the other four subspecies, Osborn's caribou (R. t. osborni), Stone's caribou (R. t. stonei), the Rocky Mountain caribou (R. t. fortidens) and the Selkirk Mountains caribou (R. t. montanus) are all montane. An extinct island dwarf subspecies,  Dawson's caribou (R. t. dawsoni), lived on Graham Island in Haida Gwaii (formerly known as the Queen Charlotte Islands).
The boreal woodland caribou (R. t. caribou), lives in the boreal forest of northeastern Canada: the Labrador caribou or Ungava caribou of Northern Quebec and northern Labrador (R. t. caboti), and the Newfoundland caribou of Newfoundland (R. t. terranovae) have been found to be genetically in the woodland caribou lineage.
In Eurasia, both wild and domestic reindeer (R. t. forma domesticus) are distributed across the tundra and into the taiga. Eurasian mountain reindeer (R. t. tarandus) are close to North American caribou genetically and visually, but with sufficient differences to warrant division into two species. grok_lead: The reindeer ( Rangifer tarandus) is a species of deer in the family Cervidae, distinguished by its circumpolar distribution across Arctic, subarctic, tundra, boreal, and alpine regions of Eurasia and North America, where it serves as a key herbivore influencing vegetation dynamics and ecosystem structure. Unique among cervids, both sexes grow large antlers annually, which are shed after the breeding season and used for foraging, defense, and social displays. Known as caribou in North America, the species exhibits remarkable adaptations to extreme cold, including a double-layered coat of dense underfur and insulating hollow guard hairs, as well as genetic modifications enabling efficient vitamin D metabolism and circadian arrhythmicity to cope with perpetual daylight or darkness. Domesticated forms have been integral to indigenous cultures, particularly among the SÃ¡mi people of northern Europe, for food, transport, clothing, and traditional livelihoods. Physically, reindeer stand 28 to 53 inches at the shoulder, with males weighing 140 to 550 pounds and females 121 to 308 pounds, enabling them to traverse deep snow and rugged terrain. Their antler s, the largest among deer, can reach 51 inches in span for males and 20 inches for females, branching asymmetrically and often used by females to protect calves from predators like wolves and bears. The species lifespan averages 15 to 18 years in the wild, though survival rates vary with environmental pressures. Genomic studies highlight further adaptations, such as mutations in the PER2 gene disrupting circadian rhythms for better activity in polar conditions and selective changes in steroid metabolism genes promoting female antler growth linked to lactation demands. Reindeer inhabit diverse northern landscapes, including open tundra, boreal forests, wetlands, and montane areas, with a range extending from Scandinavia and Russia through Iceland, Greenland, Alaska, and Canada. They are highly migratory, undertaking seasonal journeys of up to 3,000 miles between winter lichen-rich ranges and summer calving grounds to evade insects and access fresh forage, demonstrating strong site fidelity to traditional routes. As herbivores, their diet shifts seasonally: winter reliance on lichens (up to 9â18 pounds daily) and fungi, supplemented by summer vascular plants like willows, sedges, grasses, herbs, and shrubs, which they graze in herds that can number 50,000 to 500,000. This foraging behavior shapes ecosystems by preventing shrub encroachment and promoting lichen diversity, while their populations are regulated by top-down predation from wolves, bears, and eagles, and bottom-up factors like forage availability and climate. Reproduction occurs from late August to October, with a gestation of 225â235 days leading to calving in May or June, typically producing one calf per female after sexual maturity at 28â41 months. Herds exhibit social structures with matriarchal elements during migrations, and domesticated populations in Eurasia are managed by over 20 indigenous groups, integrating herding with traditional knowledge for sustainable use amid climate variability. Populations fluctuate in multidecadal cycles averaging 42 years, driven by interactions between food resources (e.g., normalized difference vegetation index) and predation, though anthropogenic disruptions like habitat fragmentation exacerbate amplitudes. Globally, wild R. tarandus is classified as Vulnerable by the IUCN as of the 2016 assessment, with a 40% decline over approximately 25 years, reducing mature individuals from about 4.8 million to 2.89 million, primarily due to habitat loss from forestry and development, unregulated hunting, climate-induced icing events, and barriers to migration. Subsequent declines have continued, with some populations dropping by up to 65% since the 1990s and projections indicating potential 50-80% global reductions by 2100 due to climate change. Subspecies vary in status, with forest and mountain forms facing the steepest declines (27â64%), while some isolated populations like Svalbard reindeer show stability or recovery through conservation. Efforts include indigenous-led monitoring, protected areas, and international agreements to mitigate threats and preserve ecological and cultural roles.
